title: Violin
summary: Not yet indistinguishable from a real violin. Pressure comes from a compact receiver and the body's modes stop at 5 kHz. E5 is too dark, A4 and B4 sound cleaner than the recording, B6 sounds 26 cents flat (the note sits on the lower of two branches that meet near the string's third, read from four probe stations), and the stopped notes B4 and B6 score below every open note. Four Dominant strings (Pickering's sections), each with two polarisations, drive a computed shell of the Guarneri il Cannone's scanned geometry in spruce and maple, with its enclosed air through an f-hole neck. The bow grips through the friction law measured on real rosin on every note but G3. B3, B4, D4, A4 and E5 use a bow of finite width with hair compliance. B4 and B6 also carry the air load on the shell's outside (the skin). E5, B3, B5, B4 and B6 sit on the audio-band maple (130 modes), with the Dominant packs' torsional loss bounded by every row of Pickering's table; A4 keeps the registered maple (134 modes), with the bounded torsional loss and the measured cross-grain loss too. On E5, B3, B5, B4 and B6 the maple's cross-grain loss is the one measured on a violin-back plate (Alkadri et al. 2018) and the receiver sits at the recording's 1.524 m; without that measured loss B5 plays the octave on the audio-band maple, and with it B5 plays its fundamental. Stopped notes press a fingertip on the string with 3.5 N; of them B3 and B4 carry a finite-width bow, and all four carry the strings' residual flexibility. The open strings are tuned to equal temperament, never to a recording. D4 and G3 play the earlier renders the 2026-11-10 restore put back, because the later renders of those notes scored below them, and both are heard through the compact receiver at 1 m: D4 the page rendered 2026-11-05, on the registered maple (134 modes) without the bounded torsional loss, the measured cross-grain loss or the measured bridge density; G3 the page shown until 2026-11-03, on the engine and card of 2026-11-01 (dda01dcbd): the registered maple (132 modes) before the corrected f-hole shape and the boundary-element neck, a bow of one contact point gripping through a Stribeck friction curve, two-gas dry air, and no longitudinal waves, skin or varnish film.
physics_present: four strings from compiled Dominant section packs (Pickering 1985), each with two transverse polarisations; all four stay coupled through the bridge while one is bowed. On every note but the restored D4 and G3 pages, which predate it, the packs carry 5e9bc150c's torsional loss factors, the torsion pendulum's own share bounded by every row of Pickering's table (E 0.003239 to 0.005454; A, D and G up 1 to 2.3 %)

a computed shell body from il Cannone's scanned geometry (Guarneri 1743) with the corrected f-hole shape (on every note but G3, whose restored page predates it): Norway spruce (Viala 2020) for the top, bass bar and soundpost, sycamore maple for the back, ribs and bridge, on the 6 mm mesh. A4 and D4 use the registered maple pack (Sonderegger 2013) and 134 modes, and G3's restored page the same pack with 132. E5, B3, B5, B4 and B6 use the audio-band maple pack (1c6c99b76): density and the in-plane stiffnesses from Lämmlein et al. 2020's violin-back plates, identified from plate modes in a 150-10000 Hz sweep, in place of Sonderegger's static values; the two transverse shear moduli and the Poisson ratio stay Sonderegger's, for want of an audio-band source. On it 130 shell modes fall inside the same 15 Hz-5 kHz window where the registered maple held 134. On every note but the restored D4 and G3 pages the maple's cross-grain (radial) loss factor is measured: 0.0240, violin-back plate C of Alkadri et al. 2018 (825ec4b44), the one plate of their twelve whose printed longitudinal loss holds Lämmlein's within its printed spread, in place of a surrogate set equal to the pack's in-plane shear loss eta_LR, 0.0162; the cross-grain viscosities rise 48 % and no frequency changes, and the two loss factors without a source (eta_LT and eta_RT) stay at that surrogate. Without the measured loss the B5 card on the audio-band maple plays the octave: over 0.5-2.4 s H2 stands 37.4 dB above H1. With it H2 stays under H1 throughout the note, 12.5 dB under over 0.5-2.4 s, where the recording's is 0.8 dB under. Between those two cards only that loss changed, besides the receiver distance, which only scales the sound. On B5, B4, B3 and B6 the bridge alone takes a measured density, 560 kg/m3, of an unmodified maple violin bridge made by Aubert (bridge No. 1 of Merhar and Humar 2020), in place of the 665.1 kg/m3 of Lämmlein et al. 2020's violin-back plates, with every stiffness and loss factor kept the back's, so the bridge loses 16 % of its mass and none of its stiffness. On A4 the bridge takes the same 560 kg/m3 in place of the registered pack's 626 kg/m3 (Sonderegger 2013), so it loses 10.5 % of its mass and none of its stiffness. On B4 the shell's outside carries a 20 µm film of an oil-copal varnish whose stiffness, loss and density Lämmlein et al. (2021) measured; the thickness is declared. The ESRF scan's own varnish meshes do not measure that film: they are a band of nearly constant depth, 6.0 voxels (0.214 mm, 0.18 to 0.25 mm on the back), and on the top the CT plate already holds all of it but the outermost voxel (0.036 mm), so the plates' scanned thickness includes the surface layer with the wood's properties. No density of il Cannone's wood is printed. CT scans of other Cremonese violins read lighter wood than the packs' 460 kg/m3 spruce and 626 or 665 kg/m3 maple: three del Gesù violins of 1734-35, tops 354 and backs 562 kg/m3 (the means of their CT medians as read from the figures of Stoel and Borman 2008 and Stoel, Borman and de Jongh 2012), the 1741 'Vieuxtemps' del Gesù 364 and 566 (Borman and Stoel, The Strad), the 1704 'Betts' Stradivari back 545 (Waddle and Sirr, The Strad 2010). But il Cannone's own measured mass, 436.6 g at 54 % RH and 21 °C (Marcon, Goli and Fioravanti 2020, who do not say whether it includes strings, pegs or a chinrest), sits with the packs: the CT part volumes at the packs' densities, with 104 to 155 g of ASSUMED parts the packs do not cover (linings and blocks, the ebony fingerboard, tailpiece, pegs, nut, saddle and strings, no chinrest; none is weighed in any source), give 417 to 483 g, and at the del Gesù densities 375 to 429 g, short of it. The ribs are 1.50 mm thick, the 10th percentile of the CT's section widths (the rib volume over the rib surface Marcon et al. measured gives 1.56 mm); Marcon et al. print 1.15 mm, averaged from the luthiers' measurements of Scrollavezza, Giordano and Montanari (1995), whose method is not printed. On the top and the back the same two routes agree within 5 %, so the difference is the ribs' alone, and the card keeps the scan. Read across the wall's own normal (a radial cut overstates the wall where it meets the rib at an angle), the same 180 CT sections give a median of 1.56 mm, 1.33 to 1.67 mm from the 10th to the 90th percentile, 36 % above the printed 1.15 mm. Neither the varnish band above (0.214 mm, if the ribs carry it as the plates do) nor the scan's excess over the authors' own CT volume, measured on the plates at a median 0.08 to 0.11 mm (0.04 to 0.18 mm across grey thresholds), would close more than about half of the 0.41 mm gap, and the rest is unexplained

the enclosed air as one cavity through a physical f-hole neck, its conductance from a boundary-element computation of the f-holes, on every note but G3, whose restored page predates that binding (0deca84189) and has the physical neck with flanged ends

on B6 and B4 (the G3 render described first, at 192 kHz, is not live: the 2026-11-10 restore put back the G3 page shown until 2026-11-03, which carries neither the skin nor the hole row): the air load on the shell's outside from a boundary-element computation (the body-radiation skin), with the f-hole neck's outer end handed to it. It changes how the body moves, not how the note is picked up. With it alone the air mode's Q is 52, against 19 printed (Jansson) and 19 without it. Nothing is dropped: the skin radiates into full space, which is right for a body this small against the wavelength, where the older compact neck end radiated into a half-space and so matched the print for the wrong reason. The viscous loss at the edge of each measured f-hole is now added on G3, each hole the circle of its own area with its own wall thickness (5.31 cm2 and 2.51 mm, 4.98 cm2 and 2.28 mm) and the air flow split between them by conductance: it takes the air mode's Q to 30 at 275.6 Hz, where the row was predicted to put it, and the rest of the gap to the printed 19 is unexplained. A control on that render's binary, the live G3 card without the hole row, reproduces the live clip byte for byte, so the change is the row's alone. B6 carries the skin and the hole row too, at 216 kHz on the audio-band maple with the measured cross-grain loss: the skin's load, computed up to 2764 Hz, now covers the note's fundamental (1946 Hz). B6 holds 7 of 15 and its pitch, and 6 by the strict ruler (5 before); its harmonic-to-noise gap narrows from 11.4 to 5.8 dB, but its attack is faster still (5.1 ms against 8.3, the recording 221), and a line near half the fundamental, at 980 Hz, rings longer: over 0.2-0.7 s it sits 30.4 dB under the fundamental, against 53.1 dB before and 65.9 dB in the recording. The same two rows, with the skin's load computed in dry air, were tried on B3, B5 and E5 on the registered maple and kept off those pages. B3 fell from 8 to 7 of 14 (the scalogram and the attack left their rulers) and E5 from 12 to 11 of 15 (the harmonics left theirs). B5 held 8 of 15, but it plays the octave: from 0.1-0.2 s on, H2 stands 16 dB above H1 where the control holds it 20.7 dB below, so its held note came out 16.3 dB under the control's while its onset (10-150 ms) fell only 4.1 dB. The skin's computed air mass lowers a body mode from 994.8 Hz by 0.71 %, onto the note's 987.8 Hz, a wolf: a bow pressed 1.5 and 2 times harder only delays the octave, to about 0.25 and 0.42 s, and at twice the force the fundamental splits into 991.0 and 1002.3 Hz, beating at 11.3 Hz. B4 carries the skin and the hole row too, in four-gas air on the varnished shell, at 216 kHz on the audio-band maple with the measured cross-grain loss; its skin load, computed up to 2764 Hz, covers that note's fundamental and 2nd to 5th harmonics. B4 holds 4 of 14 and 4 by the strict ruler, and 13 of its 15 distances to the recording shrink; its brightness gap grows and its H2 falls further under the fundamental (14.3 dB under over 0.5-2.4 s, 9.7 before), where the recording's stands above it
the steady-sliding friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13) on every note but G3, whose restored page grips through a Stribeck curve
a bow of finite width (10 mm in 3 cells) with hair compliance after Pitteroff and Woodhouse 1998, on B3, B4, D4, A4 and E5

the exact static compliance of each string's omitted modes at its bridge (residual flexibility), on the open notes G3, D4, A4 and E5, and on the stopped B3, B4, B5 and B6; on B6 also at the bow, solved with the finger stop's in one exact static Green function

a rigid fingertip pressed onto the string with 3.5 N (Issanchou et al. 2017 contact law), held by a static preload, on the stopped notes B3, B4, B5 and B6. The 3.5 N lies inside what Kinoshita and Obata (2009) measured with a force transducer in a violin's neck under the A string: the peak force exceeded 4.5 N at one and two notes per second and fell to 1.7 N at 16. The level force a slow note holds after its first pulse is not printed in the abstract, so no measured value replaces 3.5 N

longitudinal string waves on A4 (all four strings) and B3 (axial modes 1 and 2 on every string); thermochemical room air (N2, O2, Ar, CO2) on A4 and B4; dry air (N2 0.8, O2 0.2) as one gas state on the other notes
open strings tuned to equal temperament (A4 = 440 Hz) by a tension factor read from the assembled instrument's own pulse response, never from a recording
physics_missing: a radiating exterior: pressure on every page is the shell's volume and the cavity through a compact receiver, with no directivity and no finite receiver. The recording was made in an anechoic chamber with a Neumann KM 84 at 5 feet, 1.524 m (the UIowa MIS violin page). E5, B3, B5, B4 and B6 observe at that distance; the other pages (G3, D4 and A4) observe at 1 m. The compact law scales with 1/r and has no delay: on the binary that renders B5's page, a 0.25 s cut of the D4 card at 1.524 m equals the same cut at 1 m divided by 1.524 at every sample to within 0.83 LSB, the int16 rounding bound, so the distance lowers a page's raw level by 3.66 dB and changes nothing else. A directional receiver at the recording's microphone point (the one_way_observer row) was tried on G3 and refused before any sound: the shell's own triangles, which are its radiating skin, resolve six panels per wavelength only up to 2773 Hz, so a receiver that carries the whole page needs a finer CT shell mesh than the 6 mm one, and the CT data have none finer.

enough sound for the plates' motion: between about 1250 and 2000 Hz the plates move about as much per newton as Bissinger's print, within 4 dB, but give 3 to 8 dB too little sound on a finite receiver and 10 to 13 dB on the compact receiver the pages use; Bissinger's two sets reach the critical line at about 3.5 and 4.3 kHz, and the model's doesn't by 4 kHz. These reads were made on the registered maple; the audio-band maple (E5, B3, B5) has not been read this way
body modes above 5 kHz, and any mesh convergence: every page is on the 6 mm mesh, with the whole 15 Hz-5 kHz window of its maple: 134 modes on the registered maple, 130 on the audio-band maple

how near B5 sits to the octave: on the audio-band maple the B5 card plays the octave without the measured cross-grain loss and its fundamental with it. How near either card sits to the boundary between those two regimes has not been tested: there is no render between the two loss values and no step in bow force or bow speed on either card
air modes beyond the one cavity

the strings' tension loss: no printed loss exists for these strings. A web hunt found no measured bending or tension loss for the four Dominant violin strings or for any other synthetic-core violin string. The one loss row printed for a 'Dominant' cello D (Galluzzo, Woodhouse and Mansour 2017, Table 1) equals the steel-core Kaplan KS510 D3 row of Mansour, Woodhouse and Scavone (2016) to every printed digit, so it is carried over, not measured. The one measured Dominant value, Lampis (2024)'s mean Q of 1064 on a Dominant cello G, is a total loss and bounds the tension loss from above only (eta_F at most 9.0e-4).
the string-to-bridge joint's contact mechanics: an authored spring and dashpot per string (200000 N/m, 0.1 N s/m)

the second polarisation at the bridge: on every violin card each string is two-plane (`polarizations two 1 0 1 0`) and the bridge holds only the first axis (200000 N/m, 0.1 N s/m), so the second plane runs unsupported at the bridge. A support row was staged on A4 by the same law as the lateral joint (200000 N/m and 0.1 N s/m per string to a node of the bridge's shell component, an isotropic-joint assumption, with no rest offset), along each string's bridge-notch direction from the CT scan, which leans 4 to 28 degrees from vertical (G 20.9, D 3.9, A 14.0, E 28.4); a leaning row also loads the lateral plane (12000 N/m on the A string beside the joint's 200000), so ten times its stiffness is not a clean test of the vertical plane alone. It was not rendered: the same leaning row on the viola's A4 moved the eighth harmonic by 3.5 dB and ten times its stiffness moved it 4.7 dB further, and the cello's vertical row also moved with its stiffness, so a violin row would rest on a stiffness no source gives. The CT rest offsets of the strings above the nut-to-tail line (15-17 mm) are not carried: with the bridge 55 mm from the tail end they bend the afterlength to slope 0.28-0.31, outside the 0.2 slope envelope of the card's longitudinal-waves law, and without stretching a rest offset adds only a static preload

the measured bridge density on E5: the measured density of a maple violin bridge (560 kg/m3, an unmodified Aubert bridge, Merhar and Humar 2020) was rendered on the E5 card on the binary of E5's page and refused: the render stopped at 0.512 s with "friction voice refusal: active-set rescue exhausted: 5/28 pivots, last active set S-+, worst KKT violation at port 0 (slide-pos-wrong-direction-or-nondissipative) size 1e0", with the note steady (its level within 0.04 dB in every 50 ms from 0.20 s on). On the parent profile, the bridge on the back's maple, the same card renders all 3 s, so E5 keeps that page

the finite-width bow and hair compliance on the stopped notes B5 and B6. B6 was tried with the hair rows. Inside the graded first 0.7 s it rose from 7 to 8 of 15 and moved 21 c up, to -4.7 c of ET (gap to the recording 52.9 -> 31.5 c). After 0.7 s, with the bow still drawn at the card's force and speed, its level fell 20 dB under the posted page and its fundamental 22.7 dB, so H2 stands level with H1. The recording cannot show how a longer stroke behaves: its note ends near 0.6 s, and the recording is silent from 1.71 s after its onset. So B6 keeps its page. A traced 1.2 s probe of that card shows each of the 10 mm ribbon's three cells in Helmholtz motion, one fast slip per period. Between those slips the bridge-side and centre cells slip slowly about three more times per period and the far cell once. Each cell carries a third of the 0.159 N bow force. The bow is a 10 mm hair ribbon of three contact cells. On the same B6 card with the E string at 28 modes, five cells keep one fast slip per period on every cell and hold the pitch within 2 c and the level within 1 dB of three cells over 0.15-0.25 s, but harmonics 2 to 8 stand 2 to 3 dB higher against the fundamental; seven cells stop at 0.088 s (sample 12664), where the friction solver misses the one consistent contact state. So three cells is not yet shown to be converged. B5 was tried with the hair rows on its 2026-11-05 card (the registered maple) and kept that page: it renders the full 3 s without a clip, but comes out much cleaner than the recording, harmonics-to-noise 47.7 dB against 14.0 dB (19.9 dB on that page), and fell from 8 to 7 of 15. The hair rows have not been tried on B5's audio-band card.

friction beyond steady sliding: no rosin temperature and no friction memory. The thermal rosin row (Smith and Woodhouse 2000, as printed) stays off. On the bare metal string, its one-dimensional heat flow into the stationary surface, which the paper excuses only where that surface conducts little heat, holds the contact near ambient for seconds, so the bow slides at near-static friction and the note speaks late. On the rosin-shielded string that Woodhouse (2003) prints, the contact heats past the end of the measured friction curve within 0.15 s, where the row stops. Run past the 5 m/s its authors print the curve to (their extrapolated fit, not a measurement; Smith and Woodhouse keep their own runs below 40 K above ambient, "probably low enough for plausibility of this model"), D4 plays its whole stroke in Helmholtz motion: the contact passes 39.06 K above ambient only in the slip pulses, on 15 % of the sliding samples, peaking at 42.5 K, and the note comes out far cleaner than the recording (harmonics-to-noise 69 dB against 28), falling from 14 to 8 of 14.

the fingertip's own loss and contact width: the finger is a rigid point stop; printed fingertip pads (Wiertlewski and Hayward 2012) are measured on a flat plate up to 500 Hz, and no contact width on a string is printed
string modes above about 9.6 kHz on the E string, which carries 17 sines, so B6's 5th harmonic has no string mode under it
a player: constant bow speed and force, where the real E5 keeps swelling for about a second after it speaks
one co-characterised instrument: il Cannone's geometry is combined with independently sourced wood and string data
